San Francisco, Cal., Oct. An engineering task of more than ordinary interest and difficulty is that of attempting to restore the course of the Colorado River, which no longer empties into the Pacific Ocean, but has leaped its banks and is building an inland sea of its own in the Salton Sink of Southern California.

Great photographic engineers, backed by unlimited resources, are straining every fiber in a heroic effort to turn the river back into the natural bed of the waterway, but they have only a slight chance for success. Failure will drive from one of the most fertile valleys of the world 5000 prosperous farmers, whose crops and homes will be submerged under a sheet of water that will have no outlet and rival the great Salt Lake of Utah.

This new inland sea already stretches over 50 square miles of territory, and is advancing toward the higher levels at the rate of a foot a day in every direction. The Colorado River, one of the longest in the world, measuring 1,630 miles, jumped its banks few miles south of the international boundary line between California and Mexico at a dam that had been built by commercial enterprises in order to harness the river for irrigation purposes. Several million dollars were spent on the canal by private individuals. It follows the line of the Alamo River westerly, across the silt uplands of the next province known as Lower California, and then turned northward toward Imperial Valley which occupies the wedge-shaped depression between the main range of the Sierras and the Chocolate Mountain spur of the San Bernardino range.

Formerly an Inland Sea.

Oddly enough, the Salton Sink phenomena demonstrate, too, that nature, like history, frequently travels in circles of repetition. Government biologists tell us that Imperial Valley, which is now threatened with extinction by submersion, was once before, in the dim past, the bed of a great inland sea. That was centuries ago; but the fact is indelibly recorded in the stratification, which reads like an open book to the scientist. That original sea extended from the little town of Indio, some miles north of what in recent years has been designated as the Salton Sink, all the way down to the present Gulf of California. An idea of the depth of the valley may be had from the fact that half of it is even to-day lower than the level of the Pacific Ocean.

Millions of tons of silt were carried down during the centuries and deposited by the Colorado in the southern portion of the original Salton Sea. The river after a while formed a delta like that of the Nile and built a barrier which separated a portion of the inland sea from the ocean. The river gradually elevated the bed of the Colorado River higher than the sea level, and as the silt spread out over the surrounding country a lakeland was formed in that part of the Lower California peninsula known as the "overflow lands." The river cut a channel for itself down through these lands toward the Gulf of California, and the old inland sea, separated from the ocean by the newly formed overflow lands, was left without an outlet to shrink by evaporation.

Rich and Prosperous Valley.

The sea became smaller and smaller until, in our own time, nothing remained of it but the salt lake known as Salton Sink. The sink was fed by this Alamo River, flowing northward from the overflow lands, and by Crisol and San Felipe creeks, which rise in the Sierras. The sink had no outlet, and, although water was constantly entering from the river and creeks, the sink remained stationary in size because the intense heat took just as much water out of it by the process of evaporation as the entering streams brought every day.

Until few years ago Imperial Valley, south of Salton Sink, was for the most part a sage brush desert. It had once been a sea, but when the water left the region it became arid, like millions of other acres in the sultry Southwest. Civilizations advance across the Rockies brought about the application of the art of irrigation to the arid valley, and roses soon bloomed where there had been a desert waste.

In 1905 more than 1,000 acres were under irrigation in Imperial Valley, and there are now 5000 inhabitants living there on ground that is below the level of the sea. So much had been accomplished through the irrigation ditch that a company was organized for undertaking the building of a canal to recover many more thousand acres on the Mexican side of the boundary. This company spent several million dollars on the Imperial canal which harnessed the Colorado and led its waters through a dam and waterway so as to connect with the Alamo River.

Colorado Bursts Its Banks.

This irrigation canal had been completed and prospects were brightest when, suddenly, the Colorado, then at its flood height, about a year ago, smashed through the flood-gate dam of the canal and rushed toward the Alamo. Before such a torrent, with its million tons of silt every twenty-four hours, the engineers were helpless, and the turbulent waters opened the mouth of the canal a half mile, tearing great gaps out all along the artificial waterway. At Mexico the flood cut a new channel a half mile wide, and then turned northward toward Salton Sink, into which the Colorado River has since been emptying its contents, instead of following its own bed to the sea.

All of a sudden the Salton Sink—the shrunken remnant of a once wonderful inland sea—took on signs of new life and began to flood the neighboring country. That was before the Frisco earthquake, and it was some time before the natives understood the real cause. Tourists on the Transcontinental Railroad were told mysterious tales at the stations about the reason for the encroachment of the waters upon the railroad tracks. Over 100 miles of the Southern Pacific were submerged, and the tracks have been twice moved toward higher levels, but the water is still encroaching. Unless the flood is stopped the Southern Pacific will have to spend millions building a new line through the San Bernardino Mountains. That is why the Southern Pacific is spending whatever the engineers may require in an almost hopeless effort to throw the Colorado back into her channel.

Peacock was swept off his feet; nothing was too costly for him. He even hunted up his poor friends and paid their debts, and he was once a poor linen clerk.

He also owned four Pittsburgh daily newspapers and was powerful in State politics. He began life as a messenger boy.

Lovejoy, on the contrary, once a moneyless wage worker in the oil regions, first built a million dollar residence in Pittsburgh and the finest garage in Pennsylvania, then suddenly left Pittsburgh and went to Denver to live.

people of Thief River Falls will
be interested in a new law which, it is
expected, will be enacted by the Min-
nesota state legislature next winter
for the control of the liquor traffic
within the state. The features to be
embodied in these regulations are: (1)
restriction of number of saloons to be
allowed to each 1900 inhabitants of
towns and cities; (2) manner of licen-
sing same; (3) qualifications of licen-
sees; (4) limitation of brewers, distill-
ers and wholesalers from the retail
trade; (5) curtailment of the credit
system.

As to restriction, it is proposed to
classify towns and cities into two
groups according to population and to
permit one saloon for every 1900 in-
habitants in the one class and one for
every 500 in the other.

Licenses are to be issued by the dis-
trict courts instead of by city councils

hear applications and remonstrances. Appli-

and notice of application must be

est in the liquor business whatsoever.
The applicant must, moreover, be a
citizen of the United States and a
bona fide resident of the place in
which he proposes to do business.

lers, brewers and wholesalers from the
